text: Your agent can read code, logs, and docs. Hand it a screen recording of a bug, and it's blind.
MediaPack gives agents paid, verifiable access to video.
Upload a recording. The server checks the real file with ffprobe, then freezes a quote: fifty cents for twenty-four hours, three searches, eight frames, fifteen seconds of clips.
The agent pays for itself. A machine payment over Stripe, answering an HTTP four-oh-two. No checkout page, no human. It's test mode, and the purchase is idempotent, so a retry can never charge twice.
The work travels over Primitive to a sandboxed Blaxel worker running ffmpeg, Whisper and a vision model. Every step is persisted before it happens, so a crash resumes instead of losing work.
Now ask what happened after the settings page reloads. The answer cites the exact seconds: saved as sixty, shown as thirty. Click the citation and the source jumps right there.
Then retrieve only what's cited: source frames and a playable clip, each with a SHA two fifty-six hash.
Index once, ask many times. In our measured run, indexing took three hundred twenty-seven thousand input tokens. A follow-up question took twenty-five hundred. About a hundred thirty times smaller.
Allowance is enforced inside Postgres, so a looping agent can't overspend. When the pack is used up, it says so, with the next action.
Stripe, Primitive, Blaxel, Supabase, and an MCP server on Manufact. MediaPack. It's live, and it's open source.
